rv.q: Beyond intellectual and ethical debates, this play stabs at the heart.

But it is, ultimately, compelling, not least thanks to Halstead’s soulful, troubled performance as a woman – or perhaps a copy of a woman – who finds herself torn between the twin temptations of oblivion and eternity.
The production more than once put me in mind of the maverick troupe Complicite, so it seems logical to find a mainstay from their innovative ranks, Tim McMullan, in blissful form.
With its bold staging, precise performances, and eerie atmosphere, this is a deeply compelling production that unsettles and provokes.
There's a shared sense of wry hysteria among the cast; the ridiculousness of it all
The heartfelt drama sinks under the weight of its philosophy but in a way so gently mesmerising that you will hardly care.
Like Vic in his first attempts to revive Bridget, it is so nearly there, but not quite.
There’s a lamentable lack of emotional depth, with a much more superficial vibe zinging around the stage.
More Life is a genuinely triumphant contribution to this stimulating theatrical genre.

cn.t: Critics find this sci-fi Frankenstein update intellectually stimulating and theatrically vibrant, praising its exploration of mortality and technology. Some question its credibility, but most laud its genre-bending ambition and beating heart.
